*HDS MSc · Module 3 · the R version of this exercise; the web page is at <https://inflamuob.github.io/HDS_M3/day9/day6-01-importance.html>.*

*Open it in RStudio and run it a chunk at a time. Keep it in the folder that holds your `data` folder. This version has the worked answers filled in.*

Day 5 ended with a random forest that predicts diabetes well but cannot be
read like a tree or a logistic regression. The first question everyone asks of
such a model is: **which variables does it use?** This exercise answers it in
two ways, and then tests both with a column we know to be useless.

> **The plots are for looking at**
>
> The code for every plot is included, so that you can run it and see the figure. You are not expected to write it yourself.

### Packages and data

```{r}
# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "ranger", "vip"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)                   # variable importance for many kinds of model

theme_set(theme_bw())          # white background for every plot
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)     # show three significant figures in tables
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 1 — The forest

The same 750 people and five predictors as Day 5, from
[`data/diabetes_clean.csv`](data/diabetes_clean.csv): number of pregnancies,
glucose, BMI (`mass`), the diabetes pedigree function and age. As always, 80%
of the people are used for training and 20% are held back as the test set.

```{r}
diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes_clean.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split <- initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
```

A random forest of 500 trees, as on Day 5. `importance = "impurity"` asks
ranger to keep a record of how much each variable helped while it grows the
trees; Part 2 reads it. A forest is random, so set the seed first.

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("classification")

set.seed(1)
rf_fit <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)

test_preds <- test |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test, type = "prob"),
            predict(rf_fit, new_data = test))

roc_auc(test_preds, truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

The test AUC is 0.753. This is the model we explain all day. Python grows
different random trees, so its numbers differ slightly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 2 — Impurity importance

**Impurity importance** adds up, for each variable, how much purer its splits
made the training rows, over all the trees. The forest works it out while it
is fitted, so it is free. `vi()` from the **vip** package reads it.
ranger reports a raw total; divide by the sum to get each variable's share.

```{r}
vi(rf_fit) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))
```

Glucose has 0.373 of the total, then BMI 0.182, age 0.164, pedigree 0.162
and pregnancies 0.119. Glucose comes first by a long way.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 3 — Permutation importance

**Permutation importance** asks a different question: *how much worse is the
model on the test rows if one variable is scrambled?* Shuffle one column so
its values land on the wrong people, predict again, and see how much the AUC
drops. The model is not refitted.

> **Stuck?**
>
> `sample(glucose)` returns the same glucose values in a random order. Then
> predict on the shuffled test rows, `test_shuffled`.

> **Worked answer**

```{r}
set.seed(1)
test_shuffled <- test |>
  mutate(glucose = sample(glucose))

test_shuffled |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_fit, new_data = test_shuffled, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second")
```

> With glucose shuffled the AUC falls from 0.753 to 0.578, a drop of 0.175.
> Run it with another seed and the drop changes a little.

One shuffle is one random draw, so in Part 4 we repeat it 20 times for each
variable and take the average drop.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Part 4 — A control: a column of pure noise

Which measure should we believe? Test both on something whose answer we
already know: [`data/diabetes_noise.csv`](data/diabetes_noise.csv) is the same
file with one more column, `noise`: random numbers unrelated to anything. Its
true importance is **zero**.

Read it, keep `noise` as a sixth predictor, and split it exactly as before.
The same seed gives the same people in the test set.

```{r}
diabetes_noise <- read_csv("data/diabetes_noise.csv") |>
  select(pregnant, glucose, mass, pedigree, age, noise, diabetes) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

set.seed(42)
split_noise <- initial_split(diabetes_noise, prop = 0.8)
train_noise <- training(split_noise)
test_noise  <- testing(split_noise)
```

Fit the same forest on these training rows and look at its impurity
importance.

> **Stuck?**
>
> Use the training rows that contain the new column, `train_noise`. The formula
> `diabetes ~ .` picks up `noise` by itself.

> **Worked answer**

```{r}
set.seed(1)
rf_noise <- rf_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train_noise)

vi(rf_noise) |>
  mutate(share = Importance / sum(Importance))
```

> `noise` gets 0.130 of the total, fourth of six: ahead of the pedigree
> function (0.127) and pregnancies (0.109). By this measure, random numbers are
> a respectable predictor.

Now the permutation importance of the same forest on the test rows. The loop
does what you did in Part 3, 20 times for each of the six variables. Read it
line by line; it takes a few seconds.

```{r}
auc_before <- test_noise |>
  bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_noise, type = "prob")) |>
  roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
  pull(.estimate)

set.seed(1)
perm_results <- data.frame()                          # one row per shuffle

for (variable in c("pregnant", "glucose", "mass", "pedigree", "age", "noise")) {
  for (repeat_number in 1:20) {
    test_shuffled <- test_noise
    test_shuffled[[variable]] <- sample(test_shuffled[[variable]])

    auc_after <- test_shuffled |>
      bind_cols(predict(rf_noise, new_data = test_shuffled, type = "prob")) |>
      roc_auc(truth = diabetes, .pred_pos, event_level = "second") |>
      pull(.estimate)

    perm_results <- bind_rows(perm_results,
                              data.frame(variable = variable,
                                         auc_drop = auc_before - auc_after))
  }
}

perm_importance <- perm_results |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(importance = mean(auc_drop), sd = sd(auc_drop)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

perm_importance
```

```{r}
perm_importance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = importance, y = reorder(variable, importance))) +
  geom_col(fill = "coral") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = importance - sd, xmax = importance + sd),
                width = 0.3, orientation = "y") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(x = "Mean drop in test AUC when the variable is shuffled (± 1 SD)",
       y = NULL, title = "Random forest: permutation importance")
```

`noise` comes out at 0.0004, with a standard deviation of 0.009: zero, as it
should. Only glucose (0.129) and BMI (0.028) clearly beat it. The pedigree
function (0.011) is within about one standard deviation of it, and age and
pregnancies come out slightly *below* it: the forest predicts new people no
better with them than without.

Why the difference? Deep trees always find *some* split on a column with many
different values that tidies up a few training rows. Impurity importance
counts that; permutation importance on new people does not. So a variable that
does not clearly beat `noise` should not be called important.

> **Key points**
>
> - Impurity importance is free and quick, but it is computed on the training rows and is biased: it gave pure noise 13% of the total.
> - Permutation importance is the drop in test AUC when one column is shuffled. Repeat the shuffle and report the mean and spread.
> - A noise column is a control: its true importance is zero, and permutation importance puts it there.
